analysis.one_liner: Eliminates federal limits on owning a newspaper and a broadcast station in the same market.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its first House committee referral and died when the 110th Congress ended, with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the Federal Communications Commission to do away with its newspaper-broadcast cross-ownership rules, which currently prevent one company from owning both a daily newspaper and a radio or TV station in the same market [S2][S3]. The FCC would have had to finish rewriting its rules within 90 days of the bill becoming law [S3]. Removing these limits would have allowed large media companies to combine newspapers and broadcast stations under single ownership in local markets [S2][S3]. The bill was introduced in November 2007, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its telecommunications subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Large media companies and newspaper publishers that want to own both a daily newspaper and a radio or television station in the same market. Removing the cross-ownership rule would let them consolidate local news outlets into one company, reducing duplicated costs and giving a single owner control over a market's main newspaper and its broadcast news channels [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill orders the FCC to strike every provision that limits the granting or renewal of an AM or FM radio or TV license based on a party's ownership or control of a daily newspaper, freeing companies to hold both in the same market [S2][S3].
It sets a 90-day deadline for the FCC to finish the rule changes, so the deregulation would take effect quickly rather than through the commission's usual multi-year review process [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Local news audiences. When one company owns a market's dominant newspaper and its broadcast stations, there are fewer independent owners producing local news, less competition in reporting, and fewer distinct editorial voices — a cost that falls on viewers and readers rather than on any single payer [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Local news audiences and media diversity

drawbacks.text: The bill removes the main federal safeguard against a single company controlling both the major newspaper and the broadcast stations in a local market, which would concentrate local news ownership in fewer hands [S2][S3].
The bill uses a statutory mandate and a 90-day deadline to force the FCC's hand, bypassing the commission's case-by-case review of how cross-ownership affects individual markets [S3].

Even supporters of cross-ownership flexibility generally acknowledge that consolidation can mean fewer local reporters and more homogenized news content; this bill offered no replacement protections for localism or ownership diversity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow to a narrow set of large media companies, while the costs — fewer independent owners of local news outlets and less diverse coverage — are spread across everyone who relies on local news. The bill contained no offsetting protections for localism, diversity, or competition, and its 90-day FCC mandate left no room for a market-by-market review.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its telecommunications subcommittee, and it sat there until the 110th Congress ended in January 2009, never reaching a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Cliff Stearns introduced the bill on November 13, 2007; no other member cosponsored it [S1][S4].

The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and the next day to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and the Internet, where it remained with no hearings or markup [S5].
No further action was taken, and the bill expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Local news audiences are better off that the consolidation never advanced. The FCC's newspaper-broadcast cross-ownership limits remained in place during this Congress, and large media companies gained nothing from the bill's failure to move. Its death also shows how little appetite there was, even in a House where one member could introduce it freely, for undoing the rule.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Local news audiences; big media gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Cliff Stearns
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing the FCC to eliminate newspaper-broadcast cross-ownership limits

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over communications law
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to the telecommunications subcommittee, and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so no partisan divide ever formed; it simply attracted no support [S4].

industries.industry: Broadcast media companies and daily newspaper publishers
industries.note: The bill would let these companies own both a daily newspaper and radio or TV stations in the same market, consolidating a community's news sources under one owner. The industry's gain comes directly at the expense of ownership diversity and independent local news for the public [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Independent local broadcasters and small-market station owners
industries.note: Removing cross-ownership limits would let large newspaper-and-broadcast combinations move into local markets, increasing competition for independent and small operators and raising the risk that local owners are bought out or outcompeted.
